prompt: You need to test that clicking Pause while a navigation tool is still running behaves correctly. The real navigation tool finishes at unpredictable times. Best approach?
choices: Use the real tool, but wait a short fixed delay so it's mid-run when you click Pause
A `MockTool` whose `Execute` stores the callback; click Pause, then run it yourself
Run the test 10 times in CI and accept it if the large majority of runs pass
Test only the already-finished case, since the mid-run timing can't be controlled
explain: Prefer fakes over real dependencies. A mock that captures the callback lets you control exactly when work completes, so the test is deterministic, faster, and isolated from cascading failures.

prompt: A test reaches into a class with `EXPECT_EQ(object->private_state_, 42);`. The class has public `IsReady()` and `GetValue()` methods. What should the reviewer suggest?
choices: Make `private_state_` public so the test can read it without friend declarations
Add a `FRIEND_TEST` so accessing it is legal
Keep it — checking the internal field is more precise than the public getters
Assert via the public API: `IsReady()` and `GetValue() == 42`
explain: Test the API, not the implementation. Testing through public interfaces lets internals change without breaking tests, and gives other developers accurate usage examples.

prompt: A browser test checks the `Accept-Language` header on every request. The page loads subresources from several domains, and the test stores a single `std::string expected_header_`. It's flaky. Fix?
choices: Keep a per-domain map of expected values, looked up by the request's `Host`
Reset `expected_header_` after every request so stale values aren't reused
Add a short delay before setting the next expected value so requests settle
Only check the main-frame request, since subresources inherit its headers
explain: Subresource requests can arrive out of order, so a single global expected value races. Use per-domain (per-resource) expected values.

choices: The 250ms delay overshoots what's left of the window; reduce it to about 50ms instead
Use `RunUntilIdle()` instead of `NonBlockingDelay` so no wall-clock time passes
Polling eats into a timer that starts at fetch; use a far larger window, e.g. 2000ms
Start the throttle timer manually at the beginning of the test, before any polling
explain: Throttle timers start when the fetch happens, not when your checks begin, and polling waits consume that window. Use throttle times much larger than the expected polling duration.

prompt: You've drafted a fix for a flaky test that waits for a DOM update after a renderer IPC. What should you do before finalizing it?
choices: Search Chromium for tests with similar needs and reuse an established pattern
Run it 50 times locally with `--gtest_repeat`, and ship it if every run is green
Wrap it in a retry so CI reruns it automatically on an occasional failure
Disable it on the platforms where it flakes, and file a bug to investigate
explain: Before fixing async/timing issues, search the Chromium codebase for similar scenarios and prefer established, event-driven Chromium patterns over novel solutions.

prompt: Your fix uses a MutationObserver to wait for the DOM to update, an approach copied from Chromium's `service_worker_internals_ui_browsertest.cc`. What should accompany it?
choices: Nothing — a MutationObserver is self-explanatory to anyone reading the code
A link to a Stack Overflow answer explaining how MutationObserver timing works
A TODO to replace it with a simple fixed delay once the test is stable
A comment or commit note pointing at the Chromium file it's copied from
explain: When you follow a Chromium pattern, include a reference to it in a code comment or the commit message, so readers can see the precedent.

prompt:
A test contains:

```cpp
content::EvalJs(web_contents, "window.solana.isConnected");
```

What should the reviewer flag?
choices: Use `ExecJs` instead, since the script's return value isn't needed here
Check the result with `EXPECT_EQ(true, content::EvalJs(...))`
Wrap it in `base::test::RunUntil` so it retries
Nothing — `EvalJs` fails the test on JS exceptions automatically
explain: Always check `EvalJs` results with `EXPECT_TRUE`/`EXPECT_EQ`. An unchecked call swallows errors, so even a gibberish expression would "pass".

prompt: `production.cc` defines `constexpr base::TimeDelta kCleanupDelay = base::Seconds(30);` and the unit test defines an identical copy so it can advance the mock clock. Better approach?
choices: Hardcode `base::Seconds(30)` directly in the test so it reads self-contained
Keep both copies, with a comment in each pointing to the other one
Expose it once as `inline constexpr` in a shared header used by both
Advance the mock clock by a large value like 1 hour, so the exact delay doesn't matter
explain: Don't duplicate constants between production and test code. Expose the value via a shared header so both always agree.

prompt: A unit test in `//brave/components/...` gets a settings map via `HostContentSettingsMapFactory::GetForProfile(profile)` from `chrome/browser/...`. What's the right fix?
choices: Construct one directly via `base::MakeRefCounted<HostContentSettingsMap>(...)`
Add the `//chrome/browser` dep with `nogncheck`, since it's only used in tests
Move the component's test into `//brave/browser`, where profile factories are allowed
Convert it into a browser test, which provides a real profile and its factories
explain: Component unit tests must not depend on `//chrome`. If you need objects normally created by Chrome infrastructure, create them manually in the test.

choices: Add one more `FRIEND_TEST_ALL_PREFIXES` for each new test, as the class already does
Make `rename_textfield_` public, since tests are its only outside users
Add a `rename_textfield_for_testing()` accessor returning the textfield
Declare the `BraveTabTest` fixture a `friend class` and forward accessors from it
explain: When tests need a single private member, provide a `*_for_testing()` accessor returning a reference, instead of proliferating `FRIEND_TEST` macros.

choices: The global should also be reset in `TearDown()`, but otherwise the approach is sound
The test name is too long and should describe the setup rather than the outcome
Nothing — disabling stats is the simplest way to verify that no request is made
It disables the code under test, so it proves nothing; use a mock server instead
explain: When using test-only controls (globals, mocks, feature overrides), verify the test still exercises the code path it claims to test. A test that disables the code under test proves nothing.

prompt: A fixture does `void SetUp() override { g_disable_auto_start = true; }` and has no `TearDown()`. What should be added?
choices: `void TearDown() override { g_disable_auto_start = false; }`
Nothing — gtest runs each test with freshly initialized globals
Set it to `false` at the start of every other test that depends on it
Make `g_disable_auto_start` `thread_local` so it can't leak between tests
explain: If `SetUp()` disables functionality via a global, re-enable it in `TearDown()` so state doesn't leak into other tests.

prompt: A test loops over 30 URLs and runs `EXPECT_EQ(result.status, Status::kSuccess);` for each. When it fails, CI shows only `Expected kSuccess, got kError`. Improvement?
choices: Split it into 30 separate `TEST_F`s, one per URL, so the failing one is named
Stream context into it: `<< "Failed for URL: " << url << ", code: " << result.code`
Replace `EXPECT_EQ` with `ASSERT_EQ` so it stops at the first failing URL
Add `LOG(INFO) << url;` before each check so the log shows the last URL tried
explain: Include diagnostic state in assertions using `<<`, so failures can be debugged from the log without rerunning under a debugger.

prompt: A helper `VerifyTabCount(Browser*, int expected)` is called from 12 places in a browser test. When it fails, the output points only to the `EXPECT_EQ` line inside the helper. Fix?
choices: Inline the helper at every call site so each failure points at its own line
Add a `LOG(ERROR)` in the helper printing the expected and actual tab counts
Add a `base::Location` param and use `SCOPED_TRACE(location.ToString())`
Turn the helper into a macro so `__LINE__` expands at each call site instead
explain: Use `SCOPED_TRACE` with a `base::Location` defaulted to `Current()` in browser test helpers, so failure output shows the caller's file and line.

prompt: A PR adds a new AI tool handler that parses JSON arguments. Its tests cover only well-formed inputs. What should the reviewer request?
choices: Nothing — the happy path is what real users hit, and the model emits valid JSON
A browser test for the happy path too, so the full tool pipeline is exercised
A fuzzer instead of unit tests
Tests for malformed, empty, null, and out-of-range inputs
explain: Tool and handler implementations must have unit tests for bad/invalid input (malformed, empty, null, out-of-range), not just happy paths.

prompt: A refactor moves validation logic from `Parser` into a new `Validator` class. The author deletes an `EXPECT_FALSE(parser.Parse(bad_input))` check that no longer fits. Feedback?
choices: Move that check into the `Validator` tests so coverage doesn't drop
Fine — the refactor makes the check obsolete, since `Parser` no longer validates
Keep the old check commented out in the `Parser` tests for future reference
Leave it to a follow-up PR
explain: When refactoring removes a test check, move it to the appropriate new location rather than deleting it. Test coverage should never decrease during a refactor.

prompt: `GetRecentHistory()` is documented to return most-recent-first. The test checks `results.size() == 3u` and `ContainsUrl(results, ...)` for each URL. What's missing?
choices: A check that no URL appears twice, e.g. by inserting all of them into a `std::set`
Explicit order checks, e.g. `EXPECT_EQ(results[0].url, "https://c.com")`
A check that `results` isn't empty before calling `ContainsUrl` on it
Nothing — size plus `ContainsUrl` for each URL fully verifies the content
explain: When a function returns ordered data, assert the order explicitly, not just the contents.

prompt:
A test validates a serialized request body:

```cpp
EXPECT_THAT(json_str, testing::HasSubstr("\"method\":\"chain_getBlockHash\""));
```

Preferred form?
choices: Build a `base::Value::Dict` by hand with `Set("method", ...)` calls and compare it
Use `testing::MatchesRegex()` over the whole body so key order and spacing are flexible
`EXPECT_EQ(actual, base::test::ParseJsonDict(R"({"method":"chain_getBlockHash","id":1})"));`
Compare raw strings: `EXPECT_EQ(json_str, R"({"method":"chain_getBlockHash","id":1})")`
explain: Compare JSON with `base::test::ParseJsonDict()`. Never validate JSON with `HasSubstr`; it's fragile and doesn't check structure. Building dicts by hand is also discouraged.

prompt: A test for a failed title generation only checks `EXPECT_FALSE(result.has_value());`. On failure, the observer should never be told the title changed. What should be added?
choices: `EXPECT_CALL(observer, OnConversationTitleChanged(_)).WillOnce(Return())`
A second test for the success path
Nothing — the error result is enough
`EXPECT_CALL(observer, OnConversationTitleChanged(_)).Times(0);`
explain: On error/failure paths, explicitly verify that side effects which should NOT occur don't happen, e.g. with `.Times(0)`.

prompt: A deserialization test checks `title` and `url`, but the struct also has `favicon_url` and `description`. Which addition best meets the standard?
choices: Assert every field, and add a test that malformed input fails
Assert `favicon_url` only, since URL parsing is the field most likely to break
Compare `ToString()` output to a golden string
Nothing — secondary fields like `description` aren't worth dedicated assertions
explain: Serialization tests must verify ALL fields, including secondary ones like favicon URLs, and should also test deserializing invalid or malformed input.

prompt: A file has `TEST_F(MyTest, HandleTypeA)`, `HandleTypeB`, and `HandleTypeC`. Each is identical except for the input enum and the expected string. Preferred structure?
choices: Keep separate tests; they're easier to filter and each failure names its case
A table of `{name, type, expected}` cases with `SCOPED_TRACE(tc.name)`
Merge them into one test with three back-to-back `EXPECT_EQ` checks
Use a macro to stamp out the three tests so each still gets its own name
explain: For similar scenarios that differ only in inputs and outputs, use parameterized tests: a case table with `SCOPED_TRACE`, or `INSTANTIATE_TEST_SUITE_P` for larger suites.

choices: Nothing — explicit assertions at each site are more readable than helpers
Use a macro expanding to both lines, so failures still report the caller's line
Check only `is_text_content_block()`, and skip the repetitive field comparison
Extract a helper like `VerifyTextBlock(*blocks[0], "hello")`
explain: Extract repeated assertion blocks into reusable helper functions, such as `VerifyTextBlock()` and `VerifyImageBlock()`.

prompt:
```cpp
EXPECT_EQ(map[entry->uuid.value_or("")], expected_content);
```

`uuid` is a `std::optional<std::string>`. What's the better form?
choices: `EXPECT_TRUE(entry->uuid.has_value());` followed by the same `value_or("")` line
Use `entry->uuid.value()` directly, which throws if it's empty
`ASSERT_TRUE(entry->uuid.has_value());` then index with `*entry->uuid`
`value_or("missing")`, so a missing uuid yields a clearly named, failing lookup
explain: Use `ASSERT_TRUE(opt.has_value())` before accessing an optional in tests. A `value_or("")` fallback hides bugs.

prompt: An action should be blocked while the page is loading and allowed afterwards. The only test is `ActionSucceeds`, which completes loading first and then expects success. What's missing?
choices: A test that it's blocked while loading, alongside the after-loading test
A browser test version of the same happy path, to exercise real page loading
A test with a longer loading delay, so the success path is checked under load
Nothing — the success path already exercises the loading guard implicitly
explain: Test both sides of a guard condition: that the behavior is blocked while the guard is active AND that it proceeds once the guard is released.

prompt: To test error recovery, a test directly sets an object's internal members into a combination that production code can never reach, then asserts recovery works. Feedback?
choices: Good — extreme internal states make recovery tests more thorough than real ones
Fine, as long as a comment explains which internal state is being forced
Reach the scenario via production code paths; impossible states prove nothing
Wrap the setup in `#if DCHECK_IS_ON()` so it never runs in release builds
explain: Don't construct states that can't occur in production. Follow the production code path to set up the scenario; impossible-state tests give false confidence.

prompt:
`Fetch()` should be called exactly once during the test:

```cpp
EXPECT_CALL(mock, Fetch(_)).WillRepeatedly(Return(result));
```

What should change?
choices: Nothing — `WillRepeatedly` is more robust
Use `ON_CALL` instead of `EXPECT_CALL`
Add `.Times(testing::AnyNumber())`
Use `.WillOnce(Return(result))`
explain: When a mock method should be called exactly once, use `WillOnce`. `WillRepeatedly` hides bugs where it's called more times than expected.

prompt: A browser test for "open link in new tab" asserts only `EXPECT_TRUE(OpenNewTab(url));`. What should be added?
choices: An `EXPECT_CALL` on a mock tab delegate verifying it was asked to open `url`
Check the tab count went up by one and the active tab's URL is `url`
A `RunUntilIdle()` after opening so the new tab has finished loading
Nothing — `OpenNewTab` returns false whenever the tab fails to open
explain: Browser tests should verify observable side effects (the tab actually appeared, the URL actually loaded), not just return values. That catches integration issues unit tests miss.

prompt: A bug-fix PR corrects an off-by-one in tab restore. The author says existing tests pass, so no new test is needed. Response?
choices: Add a test that fails without the fix and passes with it
Agree — passing existing tests shows nothing regressed
Ask for a manual QA note in the PR description covering the restore case
A follow-up issue to add a test later is enough for a small off-by-one
explain: Every bug-fix PR should include a test reproducing the specific bug. It should fail without the fix and pass with it, guarding against regressions.

prompt: You fixed a flaky `FooTest.HandlesReload` and verified it with `--gtest_filter=FooTest.HandlesReload`. The file also has `FooTest` and `FooIncognitoTest` fixtures with other tests. What's next?
choices: Ship it — the target test passes
Run only the other `FooTest.*` tests
Run every test in the file, across all fixtures
Run the full browser_tests suite on one platform
explain: When fixing a test, run all tests in the same file across every fixture, not just the one you changed, to catch interactions between tests that share fixtures.

choices: Use `EXPECT_NE(item, nullptr)` so the failure message prints the pointer
Use `ASSERT_TRUE`/`ASSERT_NE`, since the next line dereferences `item`
Wrap `item->DoSomething()` in `if (item)` so a null item can't crash the test
Nothing — gtest stops the test at the first failed expectation anyway
explain: Use fatal `ASSERT_*` for preconditions that later code depends on. A failing `EXPECT_*` keeps running and can crash on null or cause confusing secondary failures.

prompt: A database class uses `SEQUENCE_CHECKER(sequence_checker_)`. In mock-based tests it's constructed on one sequence and used on another, so the sequence checks fail. Fix?
choices: Remove the sequence checker, since production only ever uses one sequence
Construct the object on the same sequence it's used on in every test
Wrap the checks in `#if !defined(UNIT_TEST)` so they only run in production
Call `DETACH_FROM_SEQUENCE(sequence_checker_)` in the constructor
explain: Database classes with a `SEQUENCE_CHECKER` should call `DETACH_FROM_SEQUENCE` in their constructor, so the checker binds to whichever sequence first uses the object.

choices: Drop the empty fixture and use `TEST(MyUtilsTest, ParsesValidInput)`
Add an empty `SetUp()` override so using `TEST_F` is justified
Switch to `TEST_P` so more inputs can be added later without restructuring
Nothing — `TEST_F` is always preferred, since a fixture may be needed later
explain: If the fixture adds no members, `SetUp()`, or `TearDown()`, use plain `TEST()`. `TEST_F` is only needed when the fixture provides shared state.

prompt: A test server handler serves `/api/v1` and `return nullptr;` for everything else. A code change starts hitting `/api/v2`, and the test fails mysteriously much later. Better default branch?
choices: Return a 404 response so the client sees a realistic error for unknown paths
`LOG(WARNING) << request.relative_url << request.content;` then return `nullptr`
`NOTREACHED() << "Unhandled: " << request.relative_url << request.content;`
Return an empty 200 response so the code under test keeps going
explain: Make the default handler in mock servers/interceptors `NOTREACHED() << request.content`, so unhandled requests fail loudly and the message includes the body for debugging.

prompt: Which test name follows the standard?
choices: `TEST_F(WalletServiceTest, TestSend)`
`TEST_F(WalletServiceTest, WalletServiceSendTransactionTest1)`
`TEST_F(WalletServiceTest, SendErr2)`
`TEST_F(WalletServiceTest, SendFailsOnInsufficientBalance)`
explain: Test names should be long and descriptive enough to explain the scenario without reading the body. Don't trade clarity for shorter names.

prompt: A PR adds new ranking logic with several branches but no tests. The author says it's "too hard to test because it calls the network directly; we'll add tests later." Best response?
choices: Accept it — tests can land in a follow-up once the ranking logic stabilizes
Ask for a refactor for testability (pure logic, injected deps), plus tests
Ask for a browser test that exercises the ranking against the real network
Accept it if overall project coverage stays above the 80% threshold
explain: Code that can be tested should be tested. If it's hard to test, suggest refactors that improve testability (pure functions, dependency injection, separating I/O) rather than accepting untested code.

prompt: A PR adds a settings toggle wired straight to a pref, with no other logic. A reviewer blocks it for lacking a dedicated test. Is that right?
choices: Yes — every PR that changes user-visible behavior needs at least one new test
Yes — coverage must reach 90%+ on touched lines, including UI wiring
Only if the pref is synced, since sync makes the toggle's effects cross-device
No — trivial UI with no meaningful logic doesn't need a dedicated test
explain: Use judgment: never require a dedicated test for trivial UI with no meaningful logic (like a toggle wired to a pref), or when the change follows an existing untested pattern.

prompt: You override `components/foo/foo_service.cc` via `chromium_src` and want test coverage. What's the recommended approach?
choices: Override the upstream unittest in `chromium_src`, `#include` it, then add Brave `TEST_F`s
Copy the upstream test file into brave and edit it to match the override
Write only Brave-specific tests in a new standalone fixture, unrelated to upstream's tests
Rely on upstream CI, since the upstream tests already exercise `foo_service.cc`
explain: Use the chromium_src include pattern: include the upstream test file so all upstream tests run against your override, then add Brave-specific tests reusing upstream fixtures.

prompt: A class's behavior depends on three `base::Feature` flags (`kFlagA`, `kFlagB`, `kFlagC`). How should you cover the interactions?
choices: Write three tests, each enabling one flag, since each flag is independent
Test with all flags on and with all flags off, the two extremes that matter
A value-parameterized test over `testing::Range<size_t>(0, 1 << 3)`, one bit per flag
Rely on the default flag states, and add a test whenever one of the defaults changes
explain: For multiple feature flags, use value-parameterized tests that cover all 2^N combinations, encoding each combination as a bitmask where bit `i` enables feature `i`.

prompt: Your PR flips `kMyCache` to enabled-by-default. You notice `MyCachingTest()` calls `feature_list_.InitAndEnableFeature(kMyCache)`, which is now "redundant". What should you do?
choices: Remove it — the compiled-in default now enables `kMyCache`, so it's dead code
Keep it pinned (or parameterize both states); don't rely on the default
Remove it, and add a helper that simulates the old default's behavior
Move it into `TearDown()` so it restores state after each test
explain: Tests must never rely on a `base::Feature`'s compiled-in default. Pin every flag the test depends on, or parameterize over both states, so a future default flip can't silently change coverage.

prompt: A parameterized fixture needs `ScopedFeatureList` set from `GetParam()`. Where should it be initialized?
choices: At the end of `SetUp()`, after members are created, so `GetParam()` is valid
In each `TEST_P` body, right before the code under test reads the flag value
In `TearDown()`, so the overrides are scoped to a single test
In the fixture constructor, before anything that reads the flag is constructed
explain: Initialize `ScopedFeatureList` in the fixture constructor, which runs before `SetUp()` and can already call `GetParam()`. That way nothing that reads the flag is constructed first.

prompt:
You run `brave_browser_tests --gtest_filter='AIChatPDFOCRBrowserTest.*'` and get:

```
WARNING: No matching tests to run.
SUCCESS: all tests passed.
Tests took 0 seconds.
```

What should you conclude?
choices: Nothing ran; check `--gtest_list_tests`, the target may be compiled out
The tests passed; the warning is cosmetic when the filter uses a wildcard
The tests are flaky on this machine and gtest skipped them automatically
The filter was ignored, so gtest ran and passed the full suite instead
explain: A filter that matches nothing still reports success and exits 0. Before trusting a pass, confirm the tests exist with `--gtest_list_tests` and look for `[ RUN ]`/`[ OK ]` lines with a non-zero duration.

prompt: `MyCachingTest` is instantiated with `INSTANTIATE_TEST_SUITE_P(All, MyCachingTest, testing::Bool(), ...)`. Which filter actually runs its tests?
choices: `--gtest_filter='MyCachingTest.*'`
`--gtest_filter='MyCachingTest/*'`
`--gtest_filter='All/MyCachingTest.*'`
`--gtest_filter='MyCachingTest.NotifiesWhenReady'`
explain: Parameterized suites need the instantiation prefix (`All/MyCachingTest.*`). A bare fixture-name filter matches nothing and still reports success.
